paths.title: Validation, Serialization & Error Design
paths.description: Validate every trust boundary, normalize data, serialize stable representations, distinguish domain failures, and keep error handling safe and observable.
topics: Trust-boundary validation
JSON syntax can be valid while field types, ranges, relationships, or business invariants remain invalid.
Validate external input before domain logic and reject unexpected fields when accepting them would create security or compatibility risk.
Schema validation
Executable schemas make field requirements, nullability, formats, unions, and nested structures reviewable and testable.
Use one authoritative schema per boundary and derive documentation or types from it when the tooling can preserve semantics accurately.
Normalization
Equivalent external values may need canonical casing, whitespace, date, identifier, or phone formats before comparison and storage.
Normalize only where the domain defines equivalence and preserve original user text when transformation would lose meaning.
Output filtering
Returning raw database or ORM objects can expose internal flags, secret columns, or future fields unintentionally.
Construct explicit response DTOs and allowlist properties that belong in the public contract.
Date and time serialization
Dates require explicit timezone and precision rules because local time strings are ambiguous across systems.
Use a documented instant or zoned representation such as ISO 8601/RFC 3339-compatible timestamps and keep storage/query timezone semantics consistent.
Numeric precision
JavaScript numbers cannot exactly represent every large integer or decimal financial value.
Use decimal/integer-safe representations for money, counters, and database numeric types, and document JSON encoding when values exceed safe integers.
Domain errors
Expected failures such as not-found, conflict, validation, or permission denial are different from unexpected programming defects.
Represent expected domain outcomes with stable typed errors or result values and map them centrally to transport responses.
Error redaction
Stack traces, SQL messages, internal paths, and third-party payloads can reveal sensitive implementation details.
Return safe client messages and log diagnostic detail only in protected telemetry with secret and personal-data redaction.
Correlation identifiers
A request ID connects client-visible failures to server logs and downstream traces without exposing internal diagnostics.
Generate or validate correlation IDs at the edge and propagate them through logs, calls, queues, and error envelopes.
Fail-closed behavior
Validation, authentication, or authorization uncertainty should not silently fall through to a privileged success path.
Make default-deny outcomes explicit and test malformed or missing security context as first-class failure cases.

paths.title: Relational Data Modeling & SQL
paths.description: Design tables, keys, constraints, indexes, joins, query plans, transactions, and access patterns around domain invariants rather than ORM convenience.
topics: Primary keys
A primary key gives each row stable identity and should not depend on mutable business attributes.
Choose a durable key strategy and keep externally exposed identifiers unpredictable when enumeration would create risk.
Foreign keys
Foreign keys enforce referential relationships between tables and prevent many classes of orphaned data.
Declare foreign keys for real invariants and define delete/update behavior instead of relying only on application code.
Unique constraints
Uniqueness is a database invariant and cannot be made race-safe by checking for duplicates before insert alone.
Enforce uniqueness in the database and translate constraint violations into meaningful domain conflicts.
Nullability
NULL represents missing or unknown information and interacts with comparison and uniqueness semantics differently from ordinary values.
Use NOT NULL when absence is not valid and model optionality deliberately rather than defaulting every column to nullable.
Normalization
Normalized schemas reduce duplication and update anomalies by storing facts according to their dependencies.
Normalize core entities first and denormalize only for measured read patterns with a defined consistency strategy.
Joins
INNER, LEFT, and other joins combine related rows with different inclusion semantics.
Choose joins according to the domain question and inspect cardinality so one-to-many relationships do not accidentally duplicate aggregates.
Indexes
Indexes trade storage and write cost for faster access paths on suitable predicates, joins, and ordering.
Create indexes from observed query patterns and inspect execution plans rather than indexing every column.
Query plans
The database planner chooses scans, joins, sorts, and index access based on statistics and cost estimates.
Use EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a safe environment to investigate slow queries and compare estimated versus actual row counts.
Parameterized queries
Separating SQL text from values prevents data from being interpreted as executable query syntax.
Use parameter binding for every untrusted value and never build SQL through raw string concatenation.
Database ownership boundaries
Data access becomes hard to evolve when arbitrary application code issues ad hoc queries across every table.
Encapsulate query logic behind repositories or focused data modules while still exposing transaction control where domain operations require it.
codeExamples: sql

CREATE TABLE projects (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  slug text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (owner_id, slug)
);
sql

SELECT p.id, p.slug, u.display_name
FROM projects p
JOIN users u ON u.id = p.owner_id
WHERE p.owner_id = $1
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
LIMIT $2;

paths.title: Transactions, Concurrency & Database Migrations
paths.description: Protect invariants across concurrent requests with transactions, isolation, locking, optimistic checks, safe migrations, and rollback-aware deployment sequencing.
topics: Atomic transactions
A transaction groups changes so they commit as one unit or roll back together when partial success would violate invariants.
Keep related writes in one transaction and return success only after the commit has completed.
Isolation anomalies
Concurrent transactions can observe or overwrite data in ways that depend on the database isolation level.
Identify the anomaly your domain must prevent and choose locking, isolation, or optimistic checks based on that requirement.
Lost updates
Two clients can read the same value and overwrite one another when updates do not verify the version they started from.
Use atomic SQL updates, row locks, or version columns/ETags to detect and resolve conflicting writes.
Deadlocks
Transactions that acquire locks in inconsistent orders can form cycles that the database resolves by aborting one participant.
Keep transactions short, lock resources in consistent order, and retry only the transaction classes proven safe to repeat.
Transaction boundaries
Holding a transaction open across remote calls increases lock time and couples database consistency to unreliable external latency.
Do database work in bounded units and use outbox/saga patterns when a workflow spans independent systems.
Schema migration discipline
Schema changes must coexist with old and new application versions during rolling deployments.
Use expand-and-contract migrations: add compatible structure first, deploy code that handles both states, then remove obsolete structure later.
Backfills
Large data backfills can lock tables, saturate I/O, generate replication lag, or make rollback difficult.
Backfill in bounded batches with progress markers, throttling, observability, and restart-safe idempotent logic.
Indexes on large tables
Building indexes can be expensive and may block writes depending on the database and operation mode.
Use online/concurrent index mechanisms where supported and monitor duration, locks, and replica impact.
Migration ownership
Automatically running destructive migrations from every app instance creates races and weakens deployment control.
Run migrations through a single controlled release step with explicit permissions, logs, and failure handling.
Rollback realism
Application rollback is difficult when the new release has already changed data or schema incompatibly.
Prefer backward-compatible migrations and design forward fixes for data changes that cannot be safely reversed.
codeExamples: sql
sql

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text;
-- Deploy code that reads both old/new representations, backfill safely, then enforce constraints in a later release.

paths.title: Caching, NoSQL & Storage Choices
paths.description: Choose relational, document, key-value, cache, search, object, and ephemeral stores according to consistency, query, durability, size, and access-pattern requirements.
topics: Storage selection
A datastore should match access patterns, consistency needs, durability, scale, and operational capabilities rather than trend or familiarity alone.
Write down required queries, update patterns, transaction boundaries, retention, and recovery objectives before choosing storage.
Cache purpose
A cache is a disposable faster copy of data or computation and must have a defined source of truth.
Specify cache keys, freshness, eviction, invalidation, and failure behavior before introducing a cache layer.
Cache-aside
Cache-aside loads data from the source on misses and populates the cache after successful retrieval.
Handle stale entries and thundering-herd misses explicitly, and tolerate cache loss without corrupting durable state.
Distributed cache consistency
Multiple app replicas can observe different cached values when invalidation or write ordering is weak.
Use versioned keys, bounded TTLs, pub/sub invalidation, or source revalidation according to the cost of staleness.
Key-value stores
Key-value systems excel at direct lookup and ephemeral coordination but often provide limited relational querying.
Design keys and TTL behavior from access patterns and avoid hiding complex relational requirements inside opaque serialized blobs.
Document databases
Document stores can keep aggregates together and evolve flexible records, but duplication and cross-document invariants need deliberate handling.
Choose document boundaries around atomic update needs and index actual query fields rather than storing arbitrary unqueryable JSON.
Search indexes
Search engines provide tokenization, ranking, faceting, and inverted indexes but are usually derived read models rather than authoritative stores.
Feed search from durable source events and design for eventual consistency and rebuildability.
Object storage
Object storage is suited to large immutable blobs and supports metadata, versioning, lifecycle, and signed access patterns.
Store file metadata and authorization in the application database while keeping blob bytes in object storage.
Ephemeral versus durable data
Sessions, rate-limit counters, derived caches, and job leases often have different durability requirements from business records.
Classify data by whether loss is tolerable and keep durable business truth out of stores configured only for ephemeral use.
Storage observability
Capacity, latency, hit rate, eviction, replication lag, connection saturation, and error rate reveal storage health.
Monitor metrics tied to user-facing operations and alert before resource exhaustion becomes an application outage.
codeExamples: javascript
javascript

const upload = await objectStore.createSignedUpload({ key: `users/${userId}/${fileId}`, expiresIn: 300 });
await db.files.insert({ id: fileId, ownerId: userId, objectKey: upload.key, status: "pending" });

paths.title: Authentication, Sessions & Tokens
paths.description: Establish identity safely through passwords, MFA, sessions, cookies, OAuth/OIDC, tokens, rotation, logout, recovery, and account lifecycle controls.
topics: Authentication versus authorization
Authentication establishes an identity while authorization decides what that identity may do.
Complete identity verification first and perform separate authorization checks for every protected resource and action.
Password hashing
Passwords should be processed with a slow salted password-hashing function rather than stored plaintext or reversibly encrypted.
Use a current password-hashing algorithm and parameters appropriate to the environment, and support rehashing as cost recommendations evolve.
Login throttling
Credential attacks exploit unlimited attempts across usernames, IPs, devices, or leaked password lists.
Apply risk-aware throttling and monitoring while avoiding account-lockout designs that attackers can weaponize for denial of service.
Multi-factor authentication
MFA combines independent factors and phishing-resistant authenticators provide stronger protection than easily relayed codes.
Offer or require stronger factors for sensitive accounts and design recovery so it cannot bypass the strength of normal authentication.
Session identifiers
A server session maps an opaque high-entropy identifier to authenticated server-side state.
Generate unpredictable session IDs, store them in Secure HttpOnly cookies where appropriate, rotate after privilege changes, and expire them deliberately.
Cookie attributes
Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, and lifetime settings control when session cookies are exposed or attached.
Use the narrowest cookie scope that works and understand cross-site navigation requirements before relaxing SameSite behavior.
Token validation
Signed tokens are not trusted merely because they parse; issuers, audience, algorithm, expiry, and other claims require validation.
Use vetted libraries, pin accepted algorithms and issuers, and validate every security-relevant claim before trusting token content.
OAuth and OpenID Connect
OAuth delegates authorization while OpenID Connect adds standardized identity information on top of OAuth flows.
Use authorization code flows with PKCE for public clients and validate state, nonce, redirect URIs, issuer, and audience according to the protocol.
Logout and revocation
Deleting a browser token does not revoke server sessions or long-lived credentials that remain valid elsewhere.
Terminate server-side sessions or revoke refresh credentials as required and define what logout means across devices.
Account recovery
Recovery paths are authentication paths and often become the weakest way to take over an account.
Use short-lived single-use recovery tokens, notify users of sensitive changes, and protect recovery against enumeration and social engineering.
codeExamples: javascript
res.setHeader("Set-Cookie", `session=${sessionId}; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600`);
javascript

const claims = await verifyJwt(token, { issuer: EXPECTED_ISSUER, audience: EXPECTED_AUDIENCE, algorithms: ["RS256"] });
if (!claims.sub) throw new AuthenticationError();
